topics.title: The space environment
topics.technical: Space is vacuum, extreme temperature swings, microgravity and radiation — every design constraint flows from it. Understanding the environment is the foundation of every spacecraft decision, from materials to shielding.
topics.simple: Why space is brutally hard on hardware — no air, wild temperatures, radiation.

topics.title: Orbital mechanics basics
topics.technical: Orbits are continuous free-fall governed by gravity and velocity; altitude sets period, and small burns change orbits enormously later. Kepler's laws and delta-v are the grammar of everything that flies.
topics.simple: How things stay in orbit — falling around Earth fast enough to keep missing it.

topics.title: Types of orbits
topics.technical: LEO, MEO, GEO and polar orbits each suit different missions — imaging, communications, navigation — trading coverage, latency and launch cost. Choosing the orbit is choosing the mission's shape.
topics.simple: Different heights and paths around Earth, each good for different jobs.

topics.title: Rockets and propulsion
topics.technical: Rockets throw mass backward to move forward; the rocket equation ties fuel to achievable speed, and staging beats the tyranny of carrying empty tanks. Getting to orbit is mostly a fuel-fraction problem.
topics.simple: How rockets push against nothing — and why they shed stages on the way up.

topics.title: Spacecraft subsystems
topics.technical: A spacecraft is power, thermal, propulsion, communications, attitude control and payload working together; a failure in any can end a mission. Systems thinking — how parts interact — is the core discipline.
topics.simple: The teamwork of systems — power, heat, steering, radio — that keeps a satellite alive.

topics.title: Satellites and their uses
topics.technical: Communications, Earth observation, navigation and science satellites serve distinct purposes with distinct designs. Understanding the application drives every engineering trade-off above it.
topics.simple: The different jobs satellites do — talking, watching, guiding, discovering.

topics.title: Attitude and orbit control
topics.technical: Spacecraft must point precisely — antennas at Earth, cameras at targets, panels at the Sun — using reaction wheels, thrusters and star trackers. Pointing is a control problem solved continuously.
topics.simple: Keeping a satellite aimed the right way as it hurtles through space.

topics.title: Power and thermal
topics.technical: Solar panels and batteries power spacecraft through sunlight and eclipse; radiators and heaters manage temperatures with no air to carry heat away. Energy and heat budgets constrain every design.
topics.simple: Feeding a satellite with sunlight and keeping it from freezing or cooking.

topics.title: Communications and ground stations
topics.technical: Spacecraft talk to ground stations over radio links budgeted for distance, power and noise; limited passes make autonomy and data compression essential. The link closes or the mission is deaf.
topics.simple: How we stay in radio contact with something moving thousands of km up.

topics.title: Space data and remote sensing
topics.technical: Earth-observation satellites gather imagery and sensor data across the spectrum; processing turns raw signals into maps, weather and climate insight. The value is in the data, not the hardware alone.
topics.simple: Turning what satellites see into maps, weather and climate knowledge.

topics.title: Mission design
topics.technical: A mission balances objectives, orbit, spacecraft, launch and budget against constraints; requirements flow into design and verification. Trade studies — cost vs capability vs risk — are the daily work.
topics.simple: Planning a space mission by balancing goals, physics and money.

topics.title: Launch and deployment
topics.technical: Launch vehicles carry payloads to orbit through staging and separation; deployment sequences unfold panels and antennas. The riskiest minutes of a mission's life are its first.
topics.simple: Getting to orbit and unfolding into a working satellite — the tensest part.

topics.title: CubeSats and small satellites
topics.technical: Standardised small satellites democratised space: cheaper, faster missions built by universities and startups. They trade capability for accessibility, opening space to far more players.
topics.simple: Small, cheap, standardised satellites that let almost anyone reach space.

topics.title: Radiation and reliability
topics.technical: Space radiation flips bits and degrades parts; redundancy, radiation-hardened components and error correction keep systems alive. You cannot service a satellite, so reliability is designed in, not repaired.
topics.simple: Protecting electronics from space radiation you can never send a technician to fix.

topics.title: Human spaceflight
topics.technical: Keeping humans alive adds life support, radiation shielding and psychology to every constraint; margins tighten when failure means death. The hardest missions carry people.
topics.simple: Everything gets harder when the payload is a living, breathing person.

topics.title: Deep space and exploration
topics.technical: Missions beyond Earth face long delays, autonomy, extreme distances and unforgiving windows; gravity assists and careful trajectories stretch limited fuel. Patience and precision replace real-time control.
topics.simple: Sending probes to other worlds, where commands take hours and there's no second chance.

topics.title: Space data analysis
topics.technical: Space missions generate torrents of telemetry and science data analysed with the same statistics and programming as any data field. The domain is exotic; the tools are pandas and Python.
topics.simple: Making sense of the mountains of numbers a mission sends home.

topics.title: The space industry
topics.technical: Government agencies, established primes and new commercial players form an ecosystem reshaped by falling launch costs. Understanding the industry maps where the work and the future are.
topics.simple: Who builds and flies space hardware today — and how new companies changed it.

topics.title: Space policy and sustainability
topics.technical: Orbital debris, spectrum, and international law govern a shared and crowded environment; sustainability is now an engineering constraint, not an afterthought. Space is a commons that can be ruined.
topics.simple: The rules and the growing junk problem of a crowded, shared orbit.

topics.title: Careers in space
topics.technical: Space work spans engineering, science, data, operations and business; the field rewards systems thinkers who cross disciplines. Knowing the roles maps a path into an expanding industry.
topics.simple: The many kinds of jobs in space — and how to aim at one.

topics.title: The capstone
topics.technical: Design a small satellite mission on paper: objective, orbit, subsystems, data plan and constraints, with the trade-offs justified. A coherent mission design demonstrates systems thinking end to end.
topics.simple: Design a complete small-satellite mission — proof you can think like a space engineer.
